```{r}
#| label: setup
#| include: false
Sys.setenv(TZ = "UTC")
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", message = FALSE,
                      fig.width = 7, fig.height = 4)
data_dir <- normalizePath(file.path(dirname(knitr::current_input(dir = TRUE)),
                                    "../../dev/article-data/plot-sampling"))
knitr::opts_knit$set(root.dir = data_dir)
```

The [magnitude article](magnitude-plot-sampling.html) related log tree density
to canopy height with a linear regression. Here we allow that relationship
to be nonlinear, using a Gaussian process to share information among similar
canopy heights. This uses the same process machinery as the
[spatial article](spatial-effects-plot-sampling.html), but similarity is
defined by canopy height rather than geographic distance.

We first estimate a nonlinear canopy-height relationship and predict counts
at held-out plots. In a second example, we let the slope for canopy cover
vary with canopy height. We compare both the estimated slope and the resulting
density relationships with truth. Both examples use magnitude-only models.

::: {.alert .alert-info role="note"}
**Example data**

[Download the plot-sampling data (ZIP)](downloads/plot-sampling.zip){.btn .btn-primary download="plot-sampling.zip"}

Extract it and use the folder containing `data/` as your R working directory.
We use its plot areas and canopy heights, described in the
[data article](plot-sampling-data.html), and simulate new counts below.
:::

## Simulate a nonlinear relationship

We read the 151 sampled plots and select 150 prediction cells as holdouts.
The supplied `x` column is p95 standardized using the sampled plots' mean
and standard deviation. We name it `height` here to make the formulas clear.
Standardizing also gives the process a distance scale of one standard
deviation of canopy height.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-nonlinear
library(magComp)
library(tidyverse)

set.seed(1)

plots <- read_csv("data/plots.csv") |>
  select(plot_id, area, p95, height = x)

holdout <- read_csv("data/prediction.csv") |>
  select(plot_id, area, p95, height = x) |>
  slice_sample(n = 150)
```

Let $h_i$ denote standardized canopy height. We generate expected density
$M_i$ in trees/ha and total count $N_i$ on area $a_i$ hectares from

$$
\log M_i=\log(350)-0.6\tanh(h_i),\qquad
N_i\mid M_i,r_M\sim\operatorname{NB}(a_iM_i,r_M),\qquad r_M=1000.
$$

The hyperbolic tangent, `tanh()`, describes a decrease that levels off at
shorter and taller canopy heights. At average canopy height the expected
density is 350 trees/ha. We generate counts for both sets of locations, using
only the sampled plots for fitting.

```{r}
#| label: generate-counts
plots <- plots |>
  mutate(truth = 350 * exp(-0.6 * tanh(height)),
         count = rnbinom(n(), mu = area * truth, size = 1000))

holdout <- holdout |>
  mutate(truth = 350 * exp(-0.6 * tanh(height)),
         count = rnbinom(n(), mu = area * truth, size = 1000))
```

## Fit a process over canopy height

We fit $\log M_i=\beta_0+v(h_i)$, where $v$ is a zero-mean Gaussian process.
The default exponential covariance makes effects more similar at nearby
heights. Its variance and decay are estimated. We do not supply the generating
`tanh()` relationship to the model.

```{r}
#| label: fit-nonlinear
dat <- magCompData(plots, unit = plot_id, tree_count = count,
                   design = fixedArea(area))

fit <- magComp(
  dat,
  magnitude = ~ gp(height, name = "height_effect"),
  composition = NULL,
  control = magCompControl(n_samples = 6000, n_burn = 2000,
    n_chains = 3, n_cores = 3, chain_seeds = 1:3,
    nb_size = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
)

summary(fit) |>
  select(symbol, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

Size is fixed at 1,000, following the default when magnitude has random effects.
An explicit Gamma prior can request size estimation instead, as described in
the [stratum article](stratum-effects-plot-sampling.html). We use automatic
priors and starting values for the other parameters.

The separate intercept has an R-hat of about 1.49, whereas those for the
variance and decay are close to one. As in the spatial and stratum examples,
the intercept and random effect can trade off. Their sum $\beta_0+v(h_i)$
is the log expected density at height $h_i$. We also inspect this combined
coefficient, averaged over sampled plots within each draw.

```{r}
#| label: nonlinear-combined-diagnostics
summary(fit, type = "combined", group = ".all") |>
  select(coefficient, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

The combined coefficient has an R-hat close to one, supporting its use to
describe the density relationship despite the separate intercept's slower mixing.

### Compare the estimated relationship with truth

We predict along a sequence of canopy heights. The expected target returns
draws of $M_i$, including uncertainty in the process and its parameters.
Its interval describes the mean relationship, rather than the additional
variation of a new tree count. Here `plot_id` labels evaluation points;
their heights determine the process predictions. We use 200 draws per chain
for predictions.

```{r}
#| label: predict-relationship
height_grid <- tibble(
  plot_id = 1:100,
  height = seq(min(plots$height), max(plots$height), length.out = 100)
) |>
  mutate(truth = 350 * exp(-0.6 * tanh(height)))

set.seed(1)

relationship <- predict(fit, height_grid, type = "magnitude",
                        target = "expected", summary = "samples", n_draws = 200)

relationship_summary <- summary(relationship) |>
  mutate(plot_id = as.integer(unit)) |>
  left_join(height_grid, by = "plot_id")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-nonlinear-relationship
#| fig-cap: "Expected tree density versus standardized canopy height. The blue line and band give the posterior mean and pointwise 95% credible interval; the black dashed line is the generating relationship. Gray points are observed counts divided by plot area."
ggplot(relationship_summary, aes(height, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_point(data = plots, aes(y = count / area), color = "grey50", alpha = 0.5) +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_line(aes(y = truth), linetype = "dashed") +
  labs(x = "Standardized canopy height", y = "Expected density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The estimate follows the nonlinear decrease where sampled heights are well
represented. The wide band between the shortest plot and the remaining
plots reflects how little information is available there.

### Predict held-out counts

For a new count we use the observation target, which also draws from the
negative-binomial distribution using each holdout's area. The generating
counts provide a comparison that was not available during fitting.

```{r}
#| label: predict-holdout
set.seed(1)

predictions <- predict(fit, holdout, type = "count", target = "observation",
                       summary = "samples", n_draws = 200)

prediction_summary <- summary(predictions) |>
  mutate(plot_id = as.integer(unit)) |>
  left_join(holdout, by = "plot_id")

count_limits <- c(0, max(prediction_summary$count, prediction_summary$q97_5))
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-heldout-counts
#| fig-cap: "Observed versus predicted counts for 150 holdouts. Points and bars show posterior predictive means and 95% intervals. The dashed line marks equal observed and predicted counts."
ggplot(prediction_summary, aes(count, mean)) +
  geom_abline(intercept = 0, slope = 1, linetype = "dashed", color = "grey50") +
  geom_errorbar(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), width = 0,
                color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_point(color = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.6) +
  coord_equal(xlim = count_limits, ylim = count_limits) +
  labs(x = "Observed count", y = "Predicted count") +
  theme_minimal()
```

## Let a slope vary with canopy height

A canopy-cover effect might differ between short and tall stands. The
[stratum-slope article](stratum-slopes-plot-sampling.html) let a coefficient
differ among strata; here a coefficient varies continuously with canopy height.
We reuse the plot areas and heights, simulate canopy cover between 20% and
90%, and generate new counts for this second example. With $c_i$ denoting
standardized cover, the generating model is

$$
\log M_i=\log(350)+0.2h_i+b(h_i)c_i,\qquad
b(h)=0.3-0.4\tanh(h).
$$

At fixed height, increasing cover by one standard deviation multiplies
expected density by $\exp\{b(h)\}$. Cover has a stronger positive association
with density at shorter canopy heights in this population. At average height,
$b(0)=0.3$, so this increase in cover multiplies density by $\exp(0.3)$,
about 1.35.

```{r}
#| label: simulate-varying-slope
set.seed(1)

varying_plots <- plots |>
  mutate(canopy_cover = runif(n(), 20, 90),
         cover = as.numeric(scale(canopy_cover)),
         true_slope = 0.3 - 0.4 * tanh(height),
         truth = exp(log(350) + 0.2 * height + true_slope * cover),
         count = rnbinom(n(), mu = area * truth, size = 1000))
```

We fit the model

$$
\log M_i=\beta_0+\beta_h h_i+\{\beta_c+v(h_i)\}c_i.
$$

The fixed `cover` term supplies $\beta_c$, and `cover:gp(height)` supplies
$c_i v(h_i)$. Together they estimate the cover slope $\beta_c+v(h_i)$.
In `cover:gp(height)`, `height` determines where the coefficient varies,
and `cover` multiplies that coefficient in the regression.

```{r}
#| label: fit-varying-slope
varying_dat <- magCompData(varying_plots, unit = plot_id, tree_count = count,
                           design = fixedArea(area))

varying_fit <- magComp(
  varying_dat,
  magnitude = ~ height + cover + cover:gp(height, name = "cover_slope"),
  composition = NULL,
  control = magCompControl(n_samples = 6000, n_burn = 2000,
    n_chains = 3, n_cores = 3, chain_seeds = 1:3,
    nb_size = 1000, verbose = FALSE)
)

summary(varying_fit) |>
  select(symbol, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

As with the intercept above, we inspect the combined cover slope, averaged
over sampled plots within each draw.

```{r}
#| label: slope-combined-diagnostics
summary(varying_fit, type = "combined", group = ".all") |>
  select(coefficient, mean, q2_5, q97_5, rhat, ess) |>
  knitr::kable(digits = 3)
```

### Compare true and estimated slopes

We retain predicted effects with `keep_effects = TRUE`, then use
`samples(..., type = "combined")` to add the fixed slope and process within
each draw. `cover = 0` supplies the reference cover value needed for response
prediction; the extracted coefficient is the slope itself, before it is
multiplied by cover.

```{r}
#| label: predict-slopes
slope_grid <- height_grid |>
  mutate(cover = 0, true_slope = 0.3 - 0.4 * tanh(height))

set.seed(1)

slope_predictions <- predict(varying_fit, slope_grid, type = "magnitude",
  target = "expected", summary = "samples", n_draws = 200, keep_effects = TRUE)

slope_summary <- summary(samples(slope_predictions, type = "combined")) |>
  filter(coefficient == "cover") |>
  mutate(plot_id = as.integer(unit)) |>
  left_join(slope_grid, by = "plot_id")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-varying-slope
#| fig-cap: "The canopy-cover slope as a function of standardized canopy height. Blue shows its posterior mean and pointwise 95% credible interval; the black dashed line shows the generating slope. Tick marks locate the sampled canopy heights."
ggplot(slope_summary, aes(height, mean)) +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "grey70") +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_line(aes(y = true_slope), linetype = "dashed") +
  geom_rug(data = plots, aes(x = height), inherit.aes = FALSE, alpha = 0.3) +
  labs(x = "Standardized canopy height", y = "Combined cover slope (log-density scale)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

The vertical axis is a slope on the log-density scale. Positive values mean
that greater cover is associated with higher expected density at that height;
zero means no association, and negative values mean a decrease. The estimated
slope follows the generating relationship, with greater uncertainty at heights
poorly represented by the sampled plots.

### Show the resulting density relationships

To see what these slopes imply in trees/ha, we predict expected density at
low, average, and high cover, defined as one standard deviation below the
sample mean, the mean itself, and one standard deviation above it. Each row
of the prediction table is one height--cover combination. Rows at the same
height share the predicted process effect, which is multiplied by their
respective cover values.

```{r}
#| label: predict-cover-relationships
cover_grid <- expand_grid(height = height_grid$height, cover = c(-1, 0, 1)) |>
  mutate(plot_id = row_number(),
         truth = exp(log(350) + 0.2 * height +
                       (0.3 - 0.4 * tanh(height)) * cover),
         cover_level = factor(cover, levels = c(-1, 0, 1),
           labels = c("Low cover (−1 SD)", "Average cover", "High cover (+1 SD)")))

set.seed(1)

cover_predictions <- predict(varying_fit, cover_grid, type = "magnitude",
  target = "expected", summary = "samples", n_draws = 200)

cover_summary <- summary(cover_predictions) |>
  mutate(plot_id = as.integer(unit)) |>
  left_join(cover_grid, by = "plot_id")
```

```{r}
#| label: fig-cover-relationships
#| fig-width: 8
#| fig-cap: "Expected tree density at three canopy-cover levels. Blue lines and bands show posterior means and pointwise 95% credible intervals; black dashed lines show the generating relationships. All panels use the same axes."
ggplot(cover_summary, aes(height, mean)) +
  geom_ribbon(aes(ymin = q2_5, ymax = q97_5), fill = "#0072B2", alpha = 0.2) +
  geom_line(color = "#0072B2") +
  geom_line(aes(y = truth), linetype = "dashed") +
  facet_wrap(~ cover_level, nrow = 1) +
  labs(x = "Standardized canopy height", y = "Expected density (trees/ha)") +
  theme_minimal()
```

At shorter canopy heights, the positive cover slope gives higher densities
in the high-cover panel. The differences shrink as the cover slope approaches
zero at taller heights. At average cover, $c_i=0$, so the curve depends only
on the intercept and linear height term. Its narrower band reflects uncertainty
in those coefficients; the other panels also include uncertainty in the
height-dependent cover effect.

## Extend the same ideas

`gp(height, cover)` defines a process over two covariates using Euclidean
distance. Their scales therefore matter; standardize or otherwise scale them
to express a meaningful distance before fitting. A process with identical
inputs shares one latent effect across observations. Each observation still
needs its own `unit` ID to keep its count and area separate. Shared effects
do not force equal counts or expected densities when other covariates differ.

For larger datasets, `nngp(height, m = 15)` uses the nearest-neighbor
approximation with neighbors in covariate space. Both forms support the
same varying-coefficient syntax. These terms describe covariate relationships;
geographic coordinates would be needed for an additional spatial effect.

Composition models use `factor_gp()` or `factor_nngp()` in the same way.
For example, a species formula could include
`species ~ cover + cover:factor_gp(height, K = 1, anchors = "pine")`.
The shared factor and species loadings then let cover slopes vary with height
on the probit allocation scale. The
[conditional DBH article](conditional-dbh-effects-plot-sampling.html) explains
how factor terms can also enter `dbh_class | species`.

Forest or stand summaries still use posterior predictive density draws and
area weighting with `standSummary()`, as in the
[magnitude article](magnitude-plot-sampling.html). The
[space-time article](space-time-effects-plot-sampling.html) shows how to identify
separate measurements when plots are revisited and how their effects are shared.
